claim: Host-associated microbiomes touch all facets of health.
source: Decades of research have made clear that host-associated microbiomes touch all facets of health.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact based on decades of research, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Effective therapies that target the microbiome have been elusive given its inherent complexity.
source: However, effective therapies that target the microbiome have been elusive given its inherent complexity.
evidence: This is stated as a known challenge in the field, supported by discussion of variable clinical trial outcomes.

claim: Microbiome composition influenced multiple oxalate-microbe-host interfaces.
source: Using multiple, independent molecular, rodent, and in vitro experimental models, we found that microbiome composition influenced multiple oxalate-microbe-host interfaces.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from multiple models.

claim: The administration of Oxalobacter formigenes was only effective against a poor oxalate-degrading microbiota background.
source: Importantly, the administration of the oxalate-degrading specialist, Oxalobacter formigenes, was only effective against a poor oxalate-degrading microbiota background and gives critical new insights into why clinical intervention trials with this species exhibit variable outcomes.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study supported by experimental data from microbial transplant studies.

claim: Metabolic redundancy among diverse microorganisms in specific diet-microbe axes is a critical variable that may impact the efficacy of bacteriotherapies.
source: Data suggest that, while heterogeneity in the microbiome impacts multiple diet-host-microbe interfaces, metabolic redundancy among diverse microorganisms in specific diet-microbe axes is a critical variable that may impact the efficacy of bacteriotherapies, which can help guide patient and probiotic selection criteria in probiotic clinical trials.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data showing redundancy in oxalate metabolism.

claim: Host-associated microbiomes are intimately linked to host health and touch all aspects of host physiology.
source: Decades of research have revealed that host-associated microbiomes are intimately linked to host health and touch all aspects of host physiology (Gomaa, 2020; Cox et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The first phase of microbiome research was focused on descriptive studies that characterized differences in the microbiome by host species, body site, and disease phenotypes.
source: The first phase of microbiome research was focused on descriptive studies that characterized differences in the microbiome by host species, body site, and disease phenotypes (Turnbaugh et al., 2007; Lloyd-Price et al., 2017; Wang and Jia, 2016).
evidence: This is a historical characterization of the field supported by citations.

claim: Clinical case:control metagenome-wide association studies found differences in microbiome composition between healthy and disease cohorts.
source: Clinical case:control metagenome-wide association studies that found differences in microbiome composition between healthy and disease cohorts gave rise to the ambiguous term 'dysbiosis' and much of the literature is focused on 'balancing' the gut microbiota (Tang and Hazen, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Many probiotic clinical trials with known mechanistic links between the probiotics and host physiology have exhibited wide variability in results.
source: In fact, many probiotic clinical trials, with known mechanistic links between the probiotics and host physiology, have exhibited wide variability in results (Barkhidarian et al., 2021; Rogers and Mousa, 2012; Ceccherini et al., 2022; Batagello et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple clinical trial studies.

claim: It is currently unclear what sources of variability may drive the response to targeted bacteriotherapies.
source: It is currently unclear what sources of variability may drive the response to targeted bacteriotherapies.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Heterogeneity in microbiome composition, alcohol consumption, and bowel movement quality have been proposed as variables that may drive response to targeted bacteriotherapies.
source: Some variables that have been proposed include heterogeneity in microbiome composition, alcohol consumption, and bowel movement quality (Vujkovic-Cvijin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Complex system theory is one means to potentially constrain hypotheses and bridge the gap between mechanistic studies and effective bacteriotherapies.
source: Complex system theory is one means to potentially constrain hypotheses and bridge the gap between mechanistic studies and effective bacteriotherapies (Foster et al., 2008; Layeghifard et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on complex systems.

claim: Few studies have bridged the gap between experimental biology and complex system theory.
source: Studies of the host-associated microbiome often casually acknowledge that these systems are complex and, while, there has been progress made in developing mathematical approaches to complex modeling of host-microbiome relationships (Foster et al., 2008; Layeghifard et al., 2017; Ridenhour et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2019), few studies have bridged the gap between experimental biology and complex system theory.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature despite citations showing some progress.

claim: Mammals and their gut microbiome are often considered as a holobiont.
source: Mammals and their gut microbiome, are often considered as a holobiont (Richardson, 2017), defined as a discrete unit that exhibits collective action and evolves as a unit.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The form and function of the microbial part of the holobiont is driven primarily by host-microbe influences, but which require microbe-microbe interactions to help manage the enormous burden of microbiome constraint.
source: Using evolutionary theory approaches, it is hypothesized that the form and function of the microbial part of the holobiont is driven primarily by host-microbe influences, but which require microbe-microbe interactions to help manage the enormous burden of microbiome constraint, which is termed an 'ecosystem on a leash' (Foster et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citation.

claim: Microbe-host interactions in which host-associated microbes evolve to produce metabolic by-products for the sole benefit of the host are necessarily rare.
source: Under this hypothesis, microbe-host interactions, in which host-associated microbes evolve to produce metabolic by-products for the sole benefit of the host, are necessarily rare.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the 'ecosystem on a leash' hypothesis.

claim: Essential features of complex systems include functional redundancy.
source: Essential features of complex systems include functional redundancy (Foster et al., 2017; Palla et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to complex systems literature.

claim: Essential features of complex systems include cooperation through chains of direct interactions.
source: Essential features of complex systems include functional redundancy (Foster et al., 2017; Palla et al., 2005) and cooperation through chains of direct interactions (Foster et al., 2017; Palla et al., 2005; Lambiotte et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to complex systems literature.

claim: Essential features of complex systems include distinct functional nodes that process and transfer resources.
source: Essential features of complex systems include functional redundancy (Foster et al., 2017; Palla et al., 2005) and cooperation through chains of direct interactions (Foster et al., 2017; Palla et al., 2005; Lambiotte et al., 2019), distinct functional nodes that process and transfer resources (Palla et al., 2005; Lambiotte et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to complex systems literature.

claim: Essential features of complex systems include fractality.
source: Essential features of complex systems include functional redundancy (Foster et al., 2017; Palla et al., 2005) and cooperation through chains of direct interactions (Foster et al., 2017; Palla et al., 2005; Lambiotte et al., 2019), distinct functional nodes that process and transfer resources (Palla et al., 2005; Lambiotte et al., 2019), fractality (Palla et al., 2005; Lambiotte et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to complex systems literature.

claim: Essential features of complex systems include adaptability through specific homeostatic feedback mechanisms to maintain relatively consistent internal conditions given a dynamic external environment.
source: Essential features of complex systems include functional redundancy (Foster et al., 2017; Palla et al., 2005) and cooperation through chains of direct interactions (Foster et al., 2017; Palla et al., 2005; Lambiotte et al., 2019), distinct functional nodes that process and transfer resources (Palla et al., 2005; Lambiotte et al., 2019), fractality (Palla et al., 2005; Lambiotte et al., 2019), and adaptability through specific homeostatic feedback mechanisms to maintain relatively consistent internal conditions given a dynamic external environment (Foster et al., 2017; Cohen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to complex systems literature.

claim: There is a lack of consensus on basic terminology and broadly applicable analytical or experimental models for complex systems.
source: While considerable progress has been made in understanding the nature of complex systems, there is a lack of consensus on basic terminology and broadly applicable analytical or experimental models (Torres et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Experimental evidence of multiple features of complexity within a single system is sparse, especially in microbe-host systems.
source: Thus, while some essential features of complexity have been elucidated within specific real-world systems, such as the conversion of polysaccharides to butyrate by multiple species in the gut (Roediger, 1980), or feedback loops in blood pressure regulation (Javorka et al., 2017), experimental evidence of multiple features of complexity within a single system is sparse, especially in microbe-host systems.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature with supporting citations.

claim: Antinutrients disrupt homeostasis by targeting the function of the microbiome, host, or both.
source: Antinutrients, molecules produced in plants to deter herbivory, disrupt homeostasis by targeting the function of the microbiome, host, or both (Kolodziejczyk et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Antinutrients provide an effective focal point to study complexity.
source: Antinutrients, molecules produced in plants to deter herbivory, disrupt homeostasis by targeting the function of the microbiome, host, or both (Kolodziejczyk et al., 2019), and provide an effective focal point to study complexity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the properties of antinutrients.

claim: Dietary oxalate typically provides the majority of oxalate in circulation.
source: Oxalate is an antinutrient present in many plant-based foods, which typically provides the majority of oxalate in circulation (Crivelli et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Oxalate is produced as a terminal metabolite in the liver.
source: Oxalate is an antinutrient present in many plant-based foods, which typically provides the majority of oxalate in circulation (Crivelli et al., 2020), but is also produced as a terminal metabolite in the liver (Holmes et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Some host genetic mutations increase endogenous production of oxalate.
source: While some host genetic mutations increase endogenous production of oxalate (Cochat and Rumsby, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Mammals do not produce enzymes capable of degrading oxalate.
source: While some host genetic mutations increase endogenous production of oxalate (Cochat and Rumsby, 2013), mammals do not produce enzymes capable of degrading oxalate (Hodgkinson, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Multiple oxalate-degrading bacteria exist in the gut.
source: However, multiple oxalate-degrading bacteria exist in the gut, which degrades oxalate through one of a handful of simple metabolic pathways involving one or two genes (Allison et al., 1985; Miller and Dearing, 2013; Liu et al., 2021a)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Oxalate-degrading bacteria are susceptible to antibiotics.
source: Beyond the moderate complexity, it is known that oxalate-degrading bacteria are susceptible to antibiotics and that antibiotic use decreases oxalate degradation (Nazzal et al., 2021; Miller et al., 2019b; Kharlamb et al., 2011; Lange et al., 2012; Mittal et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Antibiotic use decreases oxalate degradation.
source: Beyond the moderate complexity, it is known that oxalate-degrading bacteria are susceptible to antibiotics and that antibiotic use decreases oxalate degradation (Nazzal et al., 2021; Miller et al., 2019b; Kharlamb et al., 2011; Lange et al., 2012; Mittal et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Elevated levels of oxalate induce oxidative stress.
source: Elevated levels of oxalate induce oxidative stress, activate the inflammasome, and disrupt epithelial barrier function through tight junction proteins (Mulay et al., 2013; Peerapen and Thongboonkerd, 2011; Peerapen and Thongboonkerd, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Elevated levels of oxalate activate the inflammasome.
source: Elevated levels of oxalate induce oxidative stress, activate the inflammasome, and disrupt epithelial barrier function through tight junction proteins (Mulay et al., 2013; Peerapen and Thongboonkerd, 2011; Peerapen and Thongboonkerd, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Elevated levels of oxalate disrupt epithelial barrier function through tight junction proteins.
source: Elevated levels of oxalate induce oxidative stress, activate the inflammasome, and disrupt epithelial barrier function through tight junction proteins (Mulay et al., 2013; Peerapen and Thongboonkerd, 2011; Peerapen and Thongboonkerd, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Oxalate has been linked to kidney stones and chronic kidney disease.
source: This molecule has been linked to diseases including kidney stones and chronic kidney disease (Holmes et al., 2016; Nazzal et al., 2016; Waikar et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Oxalate has been linked to breast cancer.
source: This molecule has been linked to diseases including kidney stones and chronic kidney disease (Holmes et al., 2016; Nazzal et al., 2016; Waikar et al., 2019), breast cancer (Castellaro et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Oxalate has been linked to atherosclerosis.
source: This molecule has been linked to diseases including kidney stones and chronic kidney disease (Holmes et al., 2016; Nazzal et al., 2016; Waikar et al., 2019), breast cancer (Castellaro et al., 2015), and cardiometabolic disorders such as atherosclerosis (Liu et al., 2021b)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Oxalate has been linked to obesity.
source: This molecule has been linked to diseases including kidney stones and chronic kidney disease (Holmes et al., 2016; Nazzal et al., 2016; Waikar et al., 2019), breast cancer (Castellaro et al., 2015), and cardiometabolic disorders such as atherosclerosis (Liu et al., 2021b), obesity (Efe et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Oxalate has been linked to diabetes.
source: This molecule has been linked to diseases including kidney stones and chronic kidney disease (Holmes et al., 2016; Nazzal et al., 2016; Waikar et al., 2019), breast cancer (Castellaro et al., 2015), and cardiometabolic disorders such as atherosclerosis (Liu et al., 2021b), obesity (Efe et al., 2019), and diabetes (Efe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Oxalobacter formigenes uses oxalate as a sole carbon and energy source.
source: Oxalobacter formigenes, which uses oxalate as a sole carbon and energy source (Allison et al., 1985), is a well-studied oxalate-degrading species of bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The mechanisms of oxalate-degrading bacteria in the gut have been worked out for several decades.
source: The negative, at times lethal, effects of oxalate, along with the identification and mechanisms of oxalate-degrading bacteria in the gut, have been worked out for several decades (Allison et al., 1985; James and Butcher, 1972; Anantharam et al., 1989; Baetz and Allison, 1989; Baetz and Allison, 1990), pre-dating the current microbiome era.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature from several decades ago.

claim: Clinical intervention trials involving Oxalobacter formigenes have successfully resulted in a significant reduction in urine oxalate levels in only 43% of studies.
source: Despite this knowledge, clinical intervention trials involving Oxalobacter formigenes, which is perhaps the most effective oxalate-degrading species known, have successfully resulted in a significant reduction in urine oxalate levels in only 43% of studies (Batagello et al., 2018; Ariceta et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published meta-analyses of clinical trials.

claim: Oxalate-degrading lactic acid bacteria have been successful in 37.5% of studies.
source: Oxalate-degrading lactic acid bacteria have been successful in 37.5% of studies (Batagello et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published meta-analysis.

claim: Having an understanding of the mechanistic links between the gut microbiota and host physiology, alone, is demonstrably not sufficient to develop effective bacteriotherapies.
source: Given these data and the well worked out mechanisms of oxalate metabolism, it is clear that having an understanding of the mechanistic links between the gut microbiota and host physiology, alone, is demonstrably not sufficient to develop effective bacteriotherapies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the variable success rates of clinical trials despite known mechanisms.

claim: SW-SW mice exhibited an oxalate-dependent alteration of 219 hepatic genes, with a net increase in activity.
source: The RNAseq data analyses revealed constitutive microbiome and microbiome-dependent oxalate effects (Figure 1B and C), whereby SW-SW mice exhibited an oxalate-dependent alteration of 219 hepatic genes, with a net increase in activity
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SW-NALB mice exhibited an oxalate-dependent alteration of 21 genes with a net decrease in activity.
source: The RNAseq data analyses revealed constitutive microbiome and microbiome-dependent oxalate effects (Figure 1B and C), whereby SW-SW mice exhibited an oxalate-dependent alteration of 219 hepatic genes, with a net increase in activity, while the SW-NALB mice exhibited an oxalate-dependent alteration of 21 genes with a net decrease in activity (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In the SW-NALB mice, the primary response was a decrease in sulfation activity with oxalate exposure.
source: In the SW-NALB mice, the primary response was a decrease in sulfation activity with oxalate exposure, which is involved in the deactivation, detoxication, and excretion of xenobiotics (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of RNAseq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The primary response in the SW-SW mice was an increase in mitochondrial activity, translation, protein regulation, and ribosome biogenesis, indicative of oxalate-induced hepatic stress.
source: The primary response in the SW-SW mice was an increase in mitochondrial activity, translation, protein regulation, and ribosome biogenesis, indicative of oxalate-induced hepatic stress (Liu et al., 2021b; Strzelecki and Menon, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of RNAseq data and citations to literature on hepatic stress.

claim: Hosts only differed by gut microbiota composition in the fecal transplant experiment.
source: Since hosts only differed by gut microbiota composition, these data demonstrate causative interactions between the gut microbiota and liver activity through oxalate-dependent and independent pathways.
evidence: This is based on the experimental design using fecal transplants into genetically identical mice.

claim: The gut microbiota and liver activity interact through oxalate-dependent and independent pathways.
source: Since hosts only differed by gut microbiota composition, these data demonstrate causative interactions between the gut microbiota and liver activity through oxalate-dependent and independent pathways.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing different hepatic responses based on microbiota composition.

claim: Oxalate effectively processed within the SW-NALB gut microbiota reduced overall liver activity, indicative of a beneficial impact.
source: Within the framework of complex systems, results show microbe-host cooperation whereby oxalate effectively processed within the SW-NALB gut microbiota (Miller et al., 2019b; Miller et al., 2017a; Miller et al., 2017b; Miller et al., 2016a) reduced overall liver activity, indicative of a beneficial impact.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The SW-SW mice exhibited an alteration of 162 microbial metabolites upon oxalate exposure, with a net decrease in activity.
source: The SW-SW mice exhibited an alteration of 162 microbial metabolites upon oxalate exposure, with a net decrease in activity compared to the no oxalate group
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The SW-NALB mice exhibited an alteration of 83 microbial metabolites, with a net increase in activity.
source: The SW-SW mice exhibited an alteration of 162 microbial metabolites upon oxalate exposure, with a net decrease in activity compared to the no oxalate group, whereas the SW-NALB mice exhibited an alteration of 83 microbial metabolites, with a net increase in activity compared to the no oxalate group (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In SW-NALB mice, the primary response was an increase in lipid metabolism and a shift in fatty acid, secondary metabolite, and alkaloid profiles.
source: In SW-NALB mice, the primary response was an increase in lipid metabolism and a shift (increase/decrease) in fatty acid, secondary metabolite, and alkaloid profiles.
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of metabolomics data.

claim: In the SW-SW mice, the primary response was an increase in fatty acid synthesis and phenylalanine metabolism, and a decrease in the synthesis of secondary metabolites, cholesterol, and alkaloids.
source: In the SW-SW mice, the primary response was an increase in fatty acid synthesis and phenylalanine metabolism, and a decrease in the synthesis of secondary metabolites, cholesterol, and alkaloids (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of metabolomics data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Oxalate had a much greater impact on gut microbial metabolism in SW-SW mice overall compared to SW-NALB mice.
source: Therefore, while oxalate had a much greater impact on gut microbial metabolism in SW-SW mice overall, the metabolic pathways impacted were similar.
evidence: This is an inference from the metabolomics data showing more metabolites altered in SW-SW mice.

claim: Net changes in microbial metabolites produced are indicative of a negative impact of oxalate on microbial activity in SW-SW and a positive impact in SW-NALB mice.
source: Net changes in microbial metabolites produced are indicative of a negative impact of oxalate on microbial activity in SW-SW and a positive impact in SW-NALB mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the metabolomics data.

claim: The SW-NALB mice exhibit hallmarks of homeostatic feedback with oxalate exposure to maintain a consistent metabolic output.
source: From a complex systems perspective, data reflect a causative effect of oxalate for the shift in microbial metabolic output. Specifically, the SW-NALB mice exhibit hallmarks of homeostatic feedback with oxalate exposure to maintain a consistent metabolic output, defined by the relatively small, net negative, microbial metabolite-hepatic gene network compared to the large, net positive, network of SW-SW mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the integrated multi-omic data within a complex systems framework.

claim: Oxalate had a significant impact on metagenome composition in N. albigula.
source: Analysis of metagenomic data revealed that oxalate had a significant impact on metagenome composition (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is supported by PCoA analysis shown in Figure 3B with p=0.02.

claim: Oxalate exposure resulted in a significant increase of 1073 gene populations and a decrease of 382 gene populations in N. albigula.
source: Analysis of metagenomic data revealed that oxalate had a significant impact on metagenome composition (Figure 3B), with a significant increase of 1073 gene populations and a decrease of 382 gene populations (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by differential abundance analysis of metagenomic data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Changes in gene abundance included four oxalate metabolism gene populations in N. albigula with oxalate exposure.
source: Changes in gene abundance included four oxalate metabolism gene populations, a shift in 48 gene populations involved in formate metabolism (32+/16 -), and a shift in genes related to glycine and glyoxylate/dicarboxylate metabolism (6+/4-), which are precursors to oxalate (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of metagenomic data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Oxalate exposure resulted in a shift in 48 gene populations involved in formate metabolism in N. albigula.
source: Changes in gene abundance included four oxalate metabolism gene populations, a shift in 48 gene populations involved in formate metabolism (32+/16 -), and a shift in genes related to glycine and glyoxylate/dicarboxylate metabolism (6+/4-), which are precursors to oxalate (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of metagenomic data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A total of 128 differentially abundant genes were involved in sugar metabolism in N. albigula with oxalate exposure.
source: A total of 128 differentially abundant genes were involved in sugar metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of metagenomic data.

claim: Altered gene populations primarily belonged to O. formigenes and Alistipes senegalensis, with many genes belonging to the Muribaculum genus.
source: Altered gene populations primarily belonged to O. formigenes and Alistipes senegalensis, with many genes belonging to the Muribaculum genus (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by taxonomic mapping of differentially abundant genes shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Muribaculum spp harbor oxalate-degrading genes.
source: Muribaculum spp harbor oxalate-degrading genes, which suggests oxalate metabolic redundancy in the gut microbiota (Ormerod et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The oxalate-dependent metagenomic divergence of the NALB gut microbiota has been replicated in multiple studies.
source: The oxalate-dependent metagenomic divergence of the NALB gut microbiota (Figure 3), which has been replicated in multiple studies on the NALB gut microbiota (Miller et al., 2017a; Miller et al., 2016b)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Oxalate stimulates taxonomically diverse, but metabolically redundant microorganisms, in support of maintaining homeostasis.
source: The oxalate-dependent metagenomic divergence of the NALB gut microbiota (Figure 3), which has been replicated in multiple studies on the NALB gut microbiota (Miller et al., 2017a; Miller et al., 2016b), combined with the lack of change in the NALB microbial metabolomic profile with oxalate exposure (Figure 2, SW-NALB mice), suggest that oxalate stimulates taxonomically diverse, but metabolically redundant microorganisms, in support of maintaining homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined metagenomic and metabolomic data.

claim: The NALB microbiota is adaptive to oxalate exposure.
source: Given that data came from the same hosts sampled longitudinally, these data also reflect a microbiota that is adaptive to oxalate exposure, which is another important characteristic of complex systems, and suggests that metabolic redundancy is critical for oxalate homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference from the longitudinal metagenomic data.

claim: 59.3% of genomes extracted from N. albigula contained at least one gene associated with oxalate metabolism or handling.
source: A total of 59.3% of genomes contained at least one gene associated with oxalate metabolism or handling (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is supported by genome analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Only 27.8% of genomes harbored a complete metabolic pathway for oxalate degradation.
source: However, only 27.8% of genomes harbored a complete metabolic pathway for oxalate degradation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by genome analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Formate metabolism genes were found in 97.18% of genomes extracted from N. albigula.
source: Formate metabolism genes were found in 97.18% of genomes, which was dominated by serine hydroxymethyltransferase, and formate-tetrahydrofolate ligase (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by genome analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Acetogenic genes were present in 97.18% of genomes extracted from N. albigula.
source: Acetogenic genes were also present in 97.18% of genomes, dominated by acetate kinase and formate-tetrahydrofolate ligase (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by genome analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Methanogenic genes were present in 100% of genomes extracted from N. albigula.
source: Methanogenic genes were present in 100% of genomes, dominated by phosphoserine phosphatase, atp-dependent 6-phosphofructokinase, and phosphate acetyltransferase (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by genome analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Sulfate-reducing genes were present in 31.05% of genomes extracted from N. albigula.
source: Sulfate-reducing genes were present in 31.05% of genomes, dominated by bifunctional oligoribonuclease and PAP phosphatase, FMN reductase, and cysteine synthase (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by genome analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The broad diversity of species that contain oxalate-related genes suggests that the distribution of metabolic genes is somewhat independent of the distribution of microbial species.
source: Additionally, the broad diversity of species that contain oxalate-related genes suggests that the distribution of metabolic genes is somewhat independent of the distribution of microbial species, which suggests that microbial genes exist in an autonomous fractal layer, to some degree.
evidence: This is an inference from the genome analysis data.

claim: There is a high degree of horizontal gene transfer within the gut microbiota as a means of adaptation.
source: This hypothesis is supported by studies which show a high degree of horizontal gene transfer within the gut microbiota as a means of adaptation (Groussin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Substrates associated with metabolic pathways enriched by oxalate differentially impact oxalate metabolism in vitro.
source: Substrates associated with metabolic pathways enriched by exposure to dietary oxalate in vivo differentially impact oxalate metabolism. p<0.001 in one-way and two-way ANOVA against bacterial group and substrate
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Substrates differentially impact the influence of oxalate on microbial growth.
source: Substrates differentially impact the influence of oxalate on microbial growth; p<0.001 in two-way ANOVA against substrate and bacterial group, and one-way analysis against substrate
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both resource availability and community composition impacts oxalate metabolism.
source: Collectively, data show that both resource availability and community composition impacts oxalate metabolism, which helps to define the adaptive nature of the NALB gut microbiota.
evidence: This is an inference from the in vitro experimental data.

claim: Significant oxalate metabolism occurred even in the absence of O. formigenes, indicative of metabolic redundancy.
source: There were considerable differences in oxalate metabolism in both cohorts, dependent on the microbes present. However, significant oxalate metabolism occurred even in the absence of O. formigenes, indicative of metabolic redundancy.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: The change in urinary and fecal oxalate levels were greatest in mice given O. formigenes.
source: Using microorganisms from the taxonomic cohort, while the change in urinary and fecal oxalate levels were greatest in mice given O. formigenes, the change in oxalate levels were significantly greater than the no bacteria controls (Group 1) even in the absence of O. formigenes, consistent with in vitro results (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The change in oxalate levels were significantly greater than the no bacteria controls even in the absence of O. formigenes.
source: Using microorganisms from the taxonomic cohort, while the change in urinary and fecal oxalate levels were greatest in mice given O. formigenes, the change in oxalate levels were significantly greater than the no bacteria controls (Group 1) even in the absence of O. formigenes, consistent with in vitro results (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The change in urinary formate levels was not different in any microbial group for the taxonomic cohort.
source: Interestingly, the change in urinary formate levels was not different in any microbial group for the taxonomic cohort (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Renal CaOx deposition, cardiac fibrosis, and colitis severity all closely tracked oxalate levels.
source: Renal CaOx deposition, cardiac fibrosis, and colitis severity all closely tracked oxalate levels (Figure 6E-J, Figure 6—figure supplement 1H-I) and did not depend on O. formigenes if the other probiotic microbes were present.
evidence: This is supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 6E-J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H-I.

claim: Oxalate homeostasis and oxalate-induced pathologies are mitigated by the presence of diverse oxalate-degrading bacteria.
source: Collectively, data suggest that oxalate homeostasis and oxalate-induced pathologies are mitigated by the presence of diverse oxalate-degrading bacteria and that adding O. formigenes on an already effective oxalate-degrading microbiota will not improve oxalate homeostasis.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on in vivo experimental data.

claim: Adding O. formigenes on an already effective oxalate-degrading microbiota will not improve oxalate homeostasis.
source: Collectively, data suggest that oxalate homeostasis and oxalate-induced pathologies are mitigated by the presence of diverse oxalate-degrading bacteria and that adding O. formigenes on an already effective oxalate-degrading microbiota will not improve oxalate homeostasis.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on in vivo experimental data.

claim: The microbiota composition of colon contents was significantly different from excreted feces.
source: Based on high-throughput 16 S rRNA sequencing, the microbiota composition of colon contents from this diet trial was significantly different from excreted feces (Figure 6)
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The microbiome composition in stool from mice was not different based on probiotic administration.
source: The microbiome composition in stool from mice was not different based on probiotic administration (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Within-group differences for the All (Group 4) group was significantly lower than other groups.
source: The microbiome composition in stool from mice was not different based on probiotic administration (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), but within-group differences for the All (Group 4) group was significantly lower than other groups (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C), indicative of a protective effect against oxalate exposure.
evidence: This is supported by beta-diversity analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The microbiota of animals given the All (Group 4) group exhibited the greatest post-antibiotic recovery.
source: This conclusion is corroborated by the change in alpha diversity in which the microbiota of animals given the All (Group 4) group exhibited the greatest post-antibiotic recovery and is the only group that saw recovery beyond a marginally significant increase in diversity, post-antibiotics (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by alpha diversity analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: There was not much loss of the inoculated bacteria throughout the study, in any group.
source: In general, there was not much loss of the inoculated bacteria throughout the study, in any group (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by tracking of inoculated bacteria shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Metabolic cohort transplants were less effective than the taxonomic cohort in terms of inducing oxalate metabolism.
source: Overall, metabolic cohort transplants were less effective than the taxonomic cohort in terms of inducing oxalate metabolism, particularly in the group without bacteria (Group 1) isolated against oxalate (Figure 6B, C, Figure 6—figure supplement 3B, C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of oxalate levels between the two cohort studies.

claim: There was a much greater change in formate metabolism with the metabolic cohort, dependent on the microbes present.
source: However, there was a much greater change in format metabolism, dependent on the microbes present (Figure 6—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by formate measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3D.

claim: In both diet trials, urinary oxalate, but not formate correlated with CaOx deposition.
source: In both diet trials, urinary oxalate, but not formate correlated with CaOx deposition (Figure 6—figure supplement 3G and H – metabolic, data not shown - taxonomic).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3G and H.

claim: Oxalate's effects on both the host and the gut microbiota are primarily mediated by the metabolic redundancy of oxalate metabolism in the gut microbiota.
source: Using our complex modeling approach, our findings establish that oxalate's effects on both the host and the gut microbiota are primarily mediated by the metabolic redundancy of oxalate metabolism in the gut microbiota, rather than a single species or other factors.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the integrated experimental data.

claim: Host responses to oxalate were dependent on the composition of the gut microbiota.
source: Specifically, experiments in Figure 1 demonstrated that host responses to oxalate were dependent on the composition of the gut microbiota.
evidence: This is supported by the fecal transplant experiment showing different hepatic responses.

claim: Oxalate's impact on microbial community structure was reliant on the whole microbiota.
source: Expanding on this, experiments in Figure 2 revealed that oxalate's impact on microbial community structure was similarly reliant on the whole microbiota
evidence: This is supported by the metabolomics data showing microbiota-dependent effects.

claim: Microbial changes subsequently influenced host responses to oxalate.
source: Expanding on this, experiments in Figure 2 revealed that oxalate's impact on microbial community structure was similarly reliant on the whole microbiota, and direct multi-omic data integration confirmed that these microbial changes subsequently influenced host responses to oxalate.
evidence: This is supported by the integrated multi-omic analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The high degree of redundancy observed suggested that oxalate degradation is maintained through diverse oxalate-degrading bacteria rather than a single keystone species.
source: The high degree of redundancy observed suggested that oxalate degradation is maintained through diverse oxalate-degrading bacteria rather than a single keystone species.
evidence: This is an inference from the genome analysis showing widespread distribution of oxalate-related genes.

claim: The diversity of oxalate-degrading microbes were transferable and influenced host oxalate homeostasis more than a single species.
source: Finally, Figure 6 validated our metagenomic, metabolomic, and culturomic findings through targeted microbial transplants in mice, specifically demonstrating that the diversity of oxalate-degrading microbes were transferable and influenced host oxalate homeostasis more than a single species.
evidence: This is supported by the in vivo transplant experiments showing that diverse microbes were as effective as O. formigenes alone.

claim: Heterogeneity in microbiome composition, independent of host genetics, significantly impacted multiple diet-microbe-host interfaces.
source: Here, we found that heterogeneity in microbiome composition, independent of host genetics, significantly impacted multiple diet-microbe-host interfaces that included hepatic activity (Figures 1 and 2), gut microbiota metabolism (Figures 2 and 3), renal mineralization (Figure 6E and F; Figure 6—figure supplement 3E and F), intestinal inflammation (Figure 6H,I), and cardiac fibrosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H1).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple experiments in the study.

claim: Oxalate degradation was highly redundant among diverse species in the gut of N. albigula.
source: Importantly, we found that oxalate degradation was highly redundant among diverse species in the gut of N. albigula, which consumes a high oxalate diet in the wild (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the genome analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Administering O. formigenes led to a significant reduction in both stool and urine oxalate.
source: Consistent with past studies, administering O. formigenes led to a significant reduction in both stool and urine oxalate (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: When O. formigenes was co-administered with other oxalate-degrading microorganisms, there was no additive effect.
source: However, when co-administered with other oxalate-degrading microorganisms, there was no additive effect.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of different microbial transplant groups in the in vivo experiments.

claim: Data offer strong support for the hypothesis that metabolic redundancy among diverse taxa is the primary driver of oxalate homeostasis.
source: Collectively, data offer strong support for the hypothesis that metabolic redundancy among diverse taxa, is the primary driver of oxalate homeostasis, rather than metabolic cooperation in which the by-products of oxalate degradation are used in downstream pathways such as acetogenesis, methanogenesis, and sulfate reduction.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the integrated experimental data.

claim: Data on the metabolic cooperation hypothesis were inconclusive.
source: However, data on the metabolic cooperation hypothesis were inconclusive and there are multiple known microbe and host sources of formate, which may confound results in these studies (Asanuma et al., 1999; Hughes et al., 2017; Pietzke et al., 2020; Ternes et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study with citations to literature on formate sources.

claim: Oxalate can differentially exhibit positive or negative effects on microbial growth and metabolism dependent on the species and environment present.
source: In the current (Figures 2B and 5B) and previous studies (Allison et al., 1985; Miller and Dearing, 2013; Turroni et al., 2010; Turroni et al., 2007), we and others have found that oxalate can differentially exhibit positive or negative effects on microbial growth and metabolism dependent on the species and environment present.
evidence: This is supported by current experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The amount of oxalate consumed or produced by the liver is too great for a single, slow-growing oxalate-degrading specialist to handle alone.
source: The data showing oxalate degradation as a metabolically redundant function among multiple diverse microorganisms that maintain oxalate homeostasis (Figures 4 and 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 3), suggest that the amount of oxalate consumed or produced by the liver is too great for a single, slow-growing oxalate-degrading specialist can handle alone, in contrast to prevailing hypotheses (Daniel et al., 2021), and in support of the ecosystem on a leash hypothesis.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing metabolic redundancy.

claim: Formate is toxic to many bacterial species and to mammalian hosts.
source: In fact, multiple studies have shown that formate is toxic both to many bacterial species and to mammalian hosts, which supports this hypothesis (Hughes et al., 2017; Pietzke et al., 2020; Ternes et al., 2022; Kirkpatrick et al., 2001; Voskuhl et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The gut microbiota serves as an adaptive organ in which specific, metabolically redundant microbes respond to and eliminate dietary components.
source: Collectively, data from the current and previous studies on the effect of oxalate exposure on the gut microbiota (Miller et al., 2017a; Miller et al., 2016b) support the hypothesis that the gut microbiota serves as an adaptive organ (Scott et al., 2013; Doré and Blottière, 2015; Britton and Young, 2014) in which specific, metabolically redundant microbes respond to and eliminate dietary components, for the benefit of themselves, but which can residually protect or harm host health depending on the dietary molecules and gut microbiota composition (Tang and Hazen, 2024; Scott et al., 2013; Doré and Blottière, 2015; Britton and Young, 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by current data and citations to literature on the adaptive nature of the gut microbiota.

claim: The effects of oxalate on host health and the mechanisms of microbial oxalate degradation have largely been worked out for decades.
source: Oxalate degradation, as a focal point in diet-microbe-host interactions, is a special case in which the effects of oxalate on host health and the mechanisms of microbial oxalate degradation have largely been worked out for decades (Allison et al., 1985; James and Butcher, 1972; Anantharam et al., 1989; Baetz and Allison, 1989; Baetz and Allison, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature from several decades ago.

claim: Oxalate degradation exhibits moderate complexity, both in that it is isolated to the gut microbiota and is performed through a handful of simple metabolic pathways.
source: Furthermore, oxalate degradation exhibits moderate complexity, both in that it is isolated to the gut microbiota and is performed through a handful of simple metabolic pathways (Cochat and Rumsby, 2013; Hodgkinson, 1977; Allison et al., 1985; Miller and Dearing, 2013; Liu et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on oxalate metabolism.

claim: Understanding the mechanisms through which the gut microbiota modifies the diet to influence host health is demonstrably insufficient for the development of effective bacteriotherapies.
source: Given the complexity of diet-microbe-host interactions and the fact that understanding the mechanisms through which the gut microbiota modifies the diet to influence host health is demonstrably insufficient for the development of effective bacteriotherapies (Barkhidarian et al., 2021; Rogers and Mousa, 2012; Ceccherini et al., 2022; Batagello et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical trial studies showing variable outcomes.

claim: A three-phase, pre-clinical experimental workflow is proposed for the development of targeted bacteriotherapies.
source: Given the complexity of diet-microbe-host interactions and the fact that understanding the mechanisms through which the gut microbiota modifies the diet to influence host health is demonstrably insufficient for the development of effective bacteriotherapies (Barkhidarian et al., 2021; Rogers and Mousa, 2012; Ceccherini et al., 2022; Batagello et al., 2018), we propose a three-phase, pre-clinical experimental workflow for the development of targeted bacteriotherapies.
evidence: This is a proposal by the authors based on the findings of the study.

claim: In phase one, case:control metagenome-wide studies can identify disease phenotypes that are influenced by the microbiome.
source: In the first phase of research, case:control metagenome-wide studies and research into other factors that modify the microbiome, such as prior antibiotic exposure, can identify disease phenotypes that are influenced by the microbiome, along with the microbial taxa and genes responsible for this association.
evidence: This is part of the proposed workflow by the authors.

claim: In phase two, hypothesized taxa and/or metabolic functions can be explored through in vitro and germ-free animal studies.
source: In the second phase of research, hypothesized taxa and/or metabolic functions can be explored through in vitro and germ-free animal studies, using appropriate models to determine the mechanistic links that drive disease phenotypes through diet-microbe-host interactions.
evidence: This is part of the proposed workflow by the authors.

claim: In phase three, mechanistic links can be applied to a complex system theoretical framework to identify those variables most pertinent to successfully influence specific phenotypes.
source: Finally, in phase three, these mechanistic links can be applied to a complex system theoretical framework, as done in the current study, to identify those variables most pertinent to successfully influence specific phenotypes through targeted changes to the gut microbiota.
evidence: This is part of the proposed workflow by the authors based on the current study.

claim: A phased research structure will provide for much more effective probiotic and patient selection criteria prior to clinical trials.
source: Such a phased research structure will provide for much more effective probiotic and patient selection criteria prior to clinical trials.
evidence: This is a conclusion by the authors based on the proposed workflow.

claim: Host genetics may have an impact on oxalate homeostasis beyond the gut microbiota.
source: First, while we did conduct one study with N. albigula, most animal studies here sought to eliminate host genetics from the equation, as a means of simplification. Host genetics are another layer of complexity that were not examined here and may have an impact on oxalate homeostasis beyond the gut microbiota.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: Some batch effects are apparent in the animal studies with refined communities of microorganisms.
source: Second, in animal studies with the refined communities of microorganisms, the taxonomic and metabolic cohorts studies were conducted separately and some batch effects are apparent, such as with the change in creatinine values or urine output.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: There are multiple host and microbial sources of formate.
source: Finally, it is apparent from our data and the literature that there are multiple host and microbial sources of formate.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation affecting interpretation of formate data.

claim: The negative effects of oxalate were mitigated by metabolically redundant oxalate-degrading bacteria, more so than by metabolic cooperation or a single oxalate-degrading species.
source: In conclusion, using a complex systems theoretical framework, we examined the oxalate-microbe-host interactions of multiple oxalate-microbe-host interfaces and found multiple microbiome-dependent effects of oxalate. The negative effects of oxalate were mitigated by metabolically redundant oxalate-degrading bacteria, more so than by metabolic cooperation or a single oxalate-degrading species.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the integrated experimental data.

claim: While O. formigenes can lower urine oxalate when placed on a background of a poor oxalate-degrading community, this effect is lost when co-administered with other oxalate-degrading bacteria.
source: Critically, we found that while O. formigenes can lower urine oxalate when placed on a background of a poor oxalate-degrading community, as current theory predicts, this effect is lost when co-administered with other oxalate-degrading bacteria.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study supported by in vivo experimental data.

claim: The gut microbiota of N. albigula effectively responds to and degrades even very high dietary oxalate levels.
source: Collectively, data help to resolve why the gut microbiota of the white-throated woodrat, N. albigula, effectively responds to and degrades even very high dietary oxalate levels (Miller et al., 2017a; Miller et al., 2017b; Miller et al., 2016a)
evidence: This is supported by current data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The conceptual and experimental framework developed in this study paves the way for a phased approach to microbiome research.
source: More importantly, the conceptual and experimental framework developed in this study, based on complex systems theory, paves the way for a phased approach to microbiome research in which clinical microbiome insights (Phase I) drive mechanistic insights between the gut microbiota and host physiology (Phase II), that can be applied to a complex system model to constrain hypotheses and identify the most pertinent variables that drive microbe-host interactions that influence host physiology and health (Phase III).
evidence: This is a conclusion by the authors about the broader implications of their work.

claim: A phased approach will allow for much more efficacious probiotics and patient selection criteria in clinical intervention trials.
source: Such an approach will allow for much more efficacious probiotics and patient selection criteria in clinical intervention trials.
evidence: This is a conclusion by the authors about the implications of the proposed workflow.

claim: Swiss-Webster mice harbor a poor oxalate-degrading microbiota.
source: Specifically, Swiss-Webster mice harbor a poor oxalate-degrading microbiota and are often used in studies of hyperoxaluria (Miller et al., 2019b; Miller et al., 2017b; Miller et al., 2016a; Hatch et al., 2006; Hatch and Freel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The white-throated woodrat, Neotoma albigula, exclusively consumes Opuntia cactus, which is high in oxalate.
source: Conversely, the white-throated woodrat, Neotoma albigula, is a wild rodent that exclusively consumes Opuntia cactus, which is high in oxalate, and harbors a highly effective and responsive gut microbiota tuned to oxalate degradation (Miller et al., 2017a; Miller et al., 2014; Miller et al., 2016b; Justice, 1985; Kohl et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: N. albigula harbors a highly effective and responsive gut microbiota tuned to oxalate degradation.
source: Conversely, the white-throated woodrat, Neotoma albigula, is a wild rodent that exclusively consumes Opuntia cactus, which is high in oxalate, and harbors a highly effective and responsive gut microbiota tuned to oxalate degradation (Miller et al., 2017a; Miller et al., 2014; Miller et al., 2016b; Justice, 1985; Kohl et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neomycin effectively reduces gut microbiota density by up to 90%.
source: Neomycin is a broad spectrum antibiotic that is poorly absorbed across the gut, and effectively reduces gut microbiota density by up to 90% (Vijay-Kumar et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A 1.5% oxalate diet is sufficient to induce hyperoxaluria in Swiss-Webster mice.
source: A 1.5% oxalate diet is sufficient to induce hyperoxaluria in Swiss-Webster mice, defined as a 50% increase in urinary oxalate excretion (Miller et al., 2017b; Miller et al., 2016a; Hatch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Fecal transplants from N. albigula are sufficient to induce significant and persistent oxalate metabolism.
source: We have previously shown that fecal transplants from N. albigula are sufficient to induce significant and persistent oxalate metabolism (Miller et al., 2017b; Miller et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: 248 full-length genomes were extracted from shotgun metagenomic data from N. albigula.
source: To investigate the hypothesis that oxalate stimulates a taxonomically diverse, metabolically redundant community, 248 full-length genomes were extracted from shotgun metagenomic data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the genome extraction methods and results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 92% of genomes had at least one significantly altered gene population mapped to them with oxalate exposure.
source: A total of 92% of genomes had at least one significantly altered gene population mapped to them.
evidence: This is supported by the genome analysis shown in Figure 3E.
